File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Golden Chickens Resurfaces With Four New Malware Families and Modular Implants

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 16 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actors behind the Golden Chickens malware-as-a-service (MaaS) ecosystem have resurfaced with four new malware families, indicating that the operators are showing no signs of stopping despite extensive public disclosures into their inner workings. The malware families in question are: TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modularized variant of ChonkyChicken, and a modified web browser credential

TinyEgg ClickFix: regsvr32 executing staged .OCX payload from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the TAG-195/Golden Chickens ClickFix delivery chain where a victim pastes a Run-dialog command that downloads an OCX payload from attacker staging infrastructure and executes it with regsvr32.exe to install the TinyEgg backdoor. Article-specific because it pins regsvr32 to an .ocx from a temp/AppData/remote source, typically parented by explorer.exe (the Run-dialog hallmark of ClickFix). Rationale: Anchors on the RF-confirmed chain: ClickFix Run-dialog command downloads an OCX from staging infra and executes it via regsvr32.exe (T1218.010) — the .ocx extension + user-writable/remote path + explorer.exe parent is a tight, article-specific combination not covered by generic Office-spawns-script rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/golden-chickens-resurfaces-with-four.html • https://gbhackers.com/four-modular-malware-families/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1218.010 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers/updaters registering a bundled .ocx from a temp extraction directory (e.g. MSI custom actions)
  • Developer or QA tooling registering ActiveX controls from a build/output folder
  • Line-of-business apps that self-register OCX components on first launch under ProgramData
  • Admin scripts using regsvr32 /i with a local scriptlet during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","vc_redist.x64.exe") and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full regsvr32 command line and the OCX path/hash; check whether the parent is explorer.exe (Run-dialog paste) and look for a preceding clipboard/mshta/cmd event in the same process tree. Detonate/hash-lookup the OCX. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the regsvr32 and any child processes, and block the source staging IP/domain at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host and user for outbound WebSocket C2 to the TAG-195 infrastructure (UC2) and for Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC3), and sweep other hosts for the same OCX hash or staging domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ocx"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", "scrobj", "/i:http"))
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","mshta.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\regsvr32.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".ocx"
| where (CommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", "scrobj", "/i:http"))
     or (ParentProcessName endswith @"\explorer.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TAG-195 Golden Chickens C2 / OCX-staging infrastructure callout AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host beaconing to the confirmed TAG-195 WebSocket C2 and OCX payload-staging IPs/domains, or resolving the ClickFix lure domains. Directly ships the RF-confirmed network IOCs for TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken so an environment hit is immediately actionable. Rationale: Ships the four IPs and six domains that RF's Appendix A ties to OCX staging, WebSocket C2, and ClickFix lures — direct IOC matches are the highest-fidelity signal available for this campaign; process context (InitiatingProcess*) is projected so analysts see which binary beaconed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/golden-chickens-resurfaces-with-four.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • These are Vultr/Constant (AS20473) hosting IPs — a benign SaaS/app could later be reallocated to the same address after takedown
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment or sandbox detonation infrastructure re-contacting the domains from a research host
  • Security scanner/proxy pre-fetching a URL from an analyst's copy of the report
  • DNS sinkhole responses if the domains have been seized/sinkholed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user on the hitting host; confirm the connection is live vs. a one-off DNS resolution, and check whether the process path is a temp/AppData binary (TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all six domains and four IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: back-trace the host for the UC1 regsvr32/OCX loader and UC3 Chrome remote-debugging activity, and sweep all endpoints/DNS logs for any other resolution of these indicators over 90 days.
let c2ips = dynamic(["70.34.205.43","65.20.102.161","65.20.105.177","108.61.209.100"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["xtrafftrck.net","thessa.trackgrid.net","aurekh.com","ahdaratlegalservices.com","screenly.cam","paysolutions.ink"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DestinationIP in (c2ips) or DestinationHostName has_any (c2domains) or RequestURL has_any (c2domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChromEggscalator: off-screen Chrome/Edge remote-debugging (CDP) session hijack AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ChonkyChicken's ChromEggscalator helper launching Chrome/Edge with remote debugging enabled and positioned off-screen via negative window coordinates, then driven over the Chrome DevTools Protocol to bypass App-Bound Encryption and hijack authenticated sessions. Article-specific because it pins the exact stealth-launch combination RF described rather than generic browser abuse. Rationale: RF and the xaitax ChromElevator research confirm the exact ChromEggscalator behaviour: browser spawned off-screen (negative --window-position) with --remote-debugging-port to drive CDP and dump ABE-protected secrets — the remote-debugging + off-screen combination is far more specific than a bare browser or cookie-file read. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://github.com/xaitax/Chrome-App-Bound-Encryption-Decryption • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chonkychicken-steals-chrome-credentials/
ATT&CKT1185 T1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing (Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright) which legitimately uses --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • Developers debugging web apps against a local Chrome remote-debugging session
  • Enterprise RPA/screen-scraping tools that launch headless Chrome
  • Kiosk or CI runners that pin windows off-screen
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe","chromedriver.exe","selenium-server.exe","puppeteer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the launching parent process and the full command line — a browser parented by a temp/AppData binary or a script interpreter (not explorer.exe/CI agent) is high-signal; confirm the remote-debugging port/pipe and any negative window coordinates. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the browser + parent implant, and force-invalidate the user's web sessions (revoke refresh tokens/cookies, reset SSO sessions) since live session hijack bypasses password rotation. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 regsvr32/OCX loader and UC2 C2 callouts on the same host, and search for other endpoints where non-CI processes spawn browsers with --remote-debugging-port.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--window-position=-"
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
     or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\msedge.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\brave.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where CommandLine has "--window-position=-"
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
     or not(ParentProcessName endswith @"\chrome.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\msedge.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\explorer.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NodeBB Patches Eight AI-Found Flaws Exposing Admin Access and Private Chats

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 17 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Eight security flaws in NodeBB went public on Wednesday, along with the code to exploit them. Aikido Security rates all eight as high severity and says its AI pentest agents found them in a six-hour review of the forum software's source code. Every version before 4.14.0 is affected. NodeBB has fixed them all, and administrators should be on 4.14.2. The simplest one takes a settings change. A

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NodeBB i18n translation template-injection XSS payload in HTTP request · [LLM] NodeBB malicious ActivityPub inbox delivery burst (author spoofing / vote inflation) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NodeBB admin authorization bypass via homePageCustom rewrite to /admin routes · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NodeBB unauthenticated private-message enumeration via GET /message/:mid · [LLM] NodeBB private category content disclosure via ActivityPub outbox scrape · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
NodeBB admin authorization bypass via homePageCustom rewrite to /admin routes AIExploitation High
Hunts a non-admin forum member who sets their custom homepage (homePageCustom) to an admin path and then reaches privileged admin data endpoints (user CSV export, error log) through the home-controller rewrite, which only enforced its block client-side. Detection correlates a settings write with subsequent successful access to /api/admin/* routes from the same source. Rationale: Uses Aikido's concrete strings: the homePageCustom setting write (PUT /api/v3/users/:id/settings) and the exact exposed admin endpoints (/api/admin/users/csv, /api/admin/advanced/errors, /api/admin/manage/categories). The settings-write-then-admin-access correlation on one source IP is high-fidelity because legitimate admins never need to flip homePageCustom to reach the admin panel. Telemetry lives in web/proxy logs, not Defender AH / FDR / CloudTrail, hence those fields are empty. Corroborated Aikido writeup + CyberSecurityNews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine administrator who recently changed their own homepage preference and then opened the admin dashboard
  • Automation/monitoring account that legitimately pulls /api/admin/advanced/errors for health checks
  • QA or staging test harness exercising settings and admin routes from a shared IP
  • Admin using a bookmark that includes an /admin path stored as their landing page
Suppression filter
| where AdminUrl has_any ("/api/admin/users/csv", "/api/admin/advanced/errors", "/api/admin/manage/categories")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SrcIpAddr and resolve the NodeBB uid behind the session; confirm whether that account holds an admin role. A non-admin uid returning 200 on /api/admin/users/csv is a confirmed bypass. 2) CONTAIN: Suspend the offending forum account, invalidate its sessions, rotate any credentials exposed via the user CSV export; upgrade NodeBB to 4.14.2. 3) HUNT: Search all /api/admin/* and /admin/advanced/* access for 30d filtered to non-admin sessions; review whether the user CSV or error log was downloaded and treat exposed user data as breached.
let Lookback = 7d;
let SettingsWrites = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod == "PUT"
| where Url matches regex "(?i)/api/v3/users/[0-9]+/settings"
| project SetTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SetUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod in ("GET","POST")
| where Url has_any ("/api/admin/", "/admin/advanced/", "/admin/manage/")
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 304)
| join kind=inner SettingsWrites on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (SetTime .. SetTime + 15m)
| project SetTime, AdminAccessTime = TimeGenerated,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, SetTime),
          SrcIpAddr, SetUrl, AdminUrl = Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by AdminAccessTime desc

NodeBB unauthenticated private-message enumeration via GET /message/:mid AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts sequential enumeration of private-message IDs against GET /message/:mid, the signature-validation gap where GET requests skip verification (only POST validates), letting an attacker with no account read private conversations one ID at a time by iterating mid values. Alerts when a single source pulls many distinct message IDs in a short window. Rationale: Targets the exact Aikido vector: GET /message/:mid with skipped signature verification, exploited by iterating mid 1..80+. dcount of distinct message IDs per source per 10m window captures the systematic enumeration described by both Aikido and CyberSecurityNews while ignoring a user opening one or two of their own messages. Web-log telemetry only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user or moderator legitimately opening many of their own recent chats in a session
  • Link-preview/unfurl bot fetching several message permalinks shared elsewhere
  • NodeBB internal crawler/search-indexer walking message routes
  • Load-testing or synthetic-monitoring script hitting message endpoints
Suppression filter
| where MaxMid - MinMid >= 10 and DistinctMids >= 15
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source has no authenticated session (or a spoofed Signature keyId) and is walking a contiguous mid range; contiguous IDs with 200 responses = confirmed exploitation. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, upgrade to 4.14.2, force-rotate any secrets shared in private chats. 3) HUNT: Enumerate the full mid range the source touched to scope leaked conversations; check for the same source hitting /category/*/outbox and /api/admin/*.
let Lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where Url matches regex "(?i)/message/[0-9]+"
| extend Mid = toint(extract("/message/([0-9]+)", 1, Url))
| where isnotempty(Mid)
| summarize DistinctMids = dcount(Mid), MinMid = min(Mid), MaxMid = max(Mid),
            Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUAs = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctMids >= 15
| order by DistinctMids desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinctMsgIds values(Web.status) as statuses min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" Web.uri_path="/message/*" by Web.src _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinctMsgIds>=15
| sort - distinctMsgIds
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinctMsgIds values(Web.status) as statuses min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" Web.uri_path="/message/*" by Web.src _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinctMsgIds>=15
| sort - distinctMsgIds
NodeBB i18n translation template-injection XSS payload in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts requests carrying NodeBB translation tokens ([[namespace:key,...]]) combined with a javascript: scheme, the template-injection XSS where NodeBB renders templates before applying translations, letting attacker input smuggle translation codes that build an href and execute script on click. Fires on the token+scheme combination in the URL/query. Rationale: Uses Aikido's exact payload shape: [[topic:merged-message,javascript:alert(origin),CLICK ME]] and reflection points such as /flags?quick= and og:url meta tags. Requiring BOTH a [[ translation token (raw or %5B%5B-encoded) AND a javascript: scheme is high fidelity because that combination is never legitimate. Article's attacker.tld/4.245.3.4 IOCs dropped as PoC placeholders. Web-log only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration testers / bug-bounty researchers probing the forum
  • Automated DAST/vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei) that fuzz XSS payloads
  • Analyst manually testing the patch on 4.14.2
  • A benign forum post legitimately quoting the CVE PoC string in a security discussion thread
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Decode the RawUrl, confirm a [[...]] token wrapping a javascript: URL, and identify the reflection point (post body, /flags?quick=, profile field); check whether the response was 200. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the injected content, upgrade to 4.14.0+ (rebuilt template/translation handling), and review custom themes/plugins that may reintroduce raw-render behavior. 3) HUNT: Search stored content (posts, signatures, category descriptions) for [[ tokens containing javascript: to find persisted payloads, and review click telemetry for victims.
let Lookback = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| extend RawUrl = tostring(coalesce(UrlOriginal, Url))
| where RawUrl contains "[[" or RawUrl contains "%5B%5B" or RawUrl contains "%5b%5b"
| where RawUrl contains "javascript:" or RawUrl contains "javascript%3a" or RawUrl contains "javascript%3A"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, RawUrl, HttpStatusCode,
          HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NodeBB private category content disclosure via ActivityPub outbox scrape AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts direct pulls of NodeBB ActivityPub collection endpoints (/category/:cid/outbox, /user/:uid/outbox) which returned unfiltered posts — including private-category content — when requested with the ActivityPub Accept header, bypassing normal authorization. Focuses on browser/scripting User-Agents hitting outbox routes, indicating manual scraping rather than a legitimate federation peer. Rationale: Targets Aikido's exact endpoint (GET /category/:cid/outbox returning unfiltered private posts). Real federation peers use server User-Agents (Mastodon/http.rb/NodeBB); a browser or curl/python UA fetching /outbox is a human/scripted scrape of the ActivityPub JSON. Medium confidence because standard access logs rarely record the Accept: application/activity+json request header, so UA is the practical discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ActivityPub crawler/aggregator that presents a generic curl/Go-http User-Agent
  • Uptime or SEO monitor with a browser User-Agent hitting outbox URLs
  • Site owner testing federation endpoints from a browser
  • Search engine or archive.org fetching public category outboxes
Suppression filter
| where Url matches regex "(?i)/category/[0-9]+/outbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source pulled a category configured private/restricted and returned 200 with post content; a browser/script UA on a private /category/N/outbox = confirmed disclosure. 2) CONTAIN: Restrict federation or upgrade to 4.14.2, block the scraping source at the proxy/WAF. 3) HUNT: Enumerate which category IDs the source fetched, correlate the same IP against /message/:mid enumeration and /api/admin/* access, scope what private content left the forum.
let Lookback = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where Url matches regex "(?i)/(category/[0-9]+/outbox|user/[^/]+/outbox)"
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Mozilla", "Chrome", "Safari", "Firefox", "curl", "python", "Go-http", "okhttp")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode,
          HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NodeBB malicious ActivityPub inbox delivery burst (author spoofing / vote inflation) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts an abnormal burst of POST deliveries to NodeBB federation inbox endpoints (/inbox, /category/:cid/inbox, /user/:uid/inbox) from a single remote source — the delivery vector for CVE-2026-58593 author spoofing (attributedTo bound to a bare local uid such as 1, including the admin), Announce-wrapped Like vote inflation, and Update objects that plant XSS into the admin federation error log. Rationale: Grounded in Aikido's federation endpoints (POST /inbox, POST /category/:cid/inbox) and NVD CVE-2026-58593, which confirms an inbound actor can set attributedTo to a bare uid (e.g. 1) to author posts/DMs as any local user including admin. Access logs cannot inspect the ActivityPub JSON body, so this catches the observable delivery-burst pattern rather than object contents — Medium confidence; pair with NodeBB federation/error logs for body-level confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58593
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Popular federated account whose posts legitimately fan out to many inbox deliveries
  • Mastodon/relay backfill after a new follow generates a delivery burst
  • Federation relay retrying failed deliveries
  • Legitimate high-traffic remote instance during peak activity
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the NodeBB federation/error log for the same window and inspect ActivityPub objects from this source for attributedTo bound to a bare local uid, Announce wrappers with mismatched object.actor, or Update ids containing HTML — any confirms exploitation. 2) CONTAIN: Defederate/block the remote actor and its IP, upgrade to 4.14.2 (binds author to verified signature), audit posts/DMs recently attributed to admin/privileged uids. 3) HUNT: Review vote counts on targeted posts for inflation, check the admin federation error-log page for stored XSS, remove forged content authored via spoofed attributedTo.
let Lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url matches regex "(?i)/(inbox|category/[0-9]+/inbox|user/[^/]+/inbox)"
| summarize PostCount = count(), DistinctInboxes = dcount(Url),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 8), SampleUA = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 3)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where PostCount >= 20
| order by PostCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinctInboxes values(Web.uri_path) as inboxes values(Web.http_user_agent) as uas min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" (Web.uri_path="*/inbox" OR Web.uri_path="/inbox") by Web.src _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count>=20
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinctInboxes values(Web.uri_path) as inboxes values(Web.http_user_agent) as uas min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" (Web.uri_path="*/inbox" OR Web.uri_path="/inbox") by Web.src _time span=10m

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Kimi K3 Agents Found Redis Zero-Days and Built RCE Exploit, Researchers Say

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 15 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Redis shipped seven security releases on July 23 after researchers published authenticated RCE PoCs for stock Redis 6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, and 8.8.0. All four chains require RESTORE. The Streams chains also need EVAL and XGROUP; the 8.8.0 chain needs EVAL and the bundled RedisBloom module. Redis says the underlying memory flaws may lead to remote code execution. redis-server process spawning a shell or interpreter (RESTORE RCE system() payoff) AIExploitation High
Hunts the code-execution payoff of the July 2026 Redis RESTORE chains (Streams shared-NACK UAF and RedisBloom/TDigest OOB write), which all culminate in the redis-server process calling system(). A redis-server parent spawning sh/bash/python/nc/ssh is the smoking-gun observable regardless of which of the four memory-corruption chains was used. Rationale: redis-server should never fork a shell/interpreter in normal operation; every disclosed chain ends in system() invoked from the redis process, making parent=redis-server + child-shell the single most reliable observable. Corroborated against the Redis advisory and berabuddies PoC repo. Datadog left empty: linux.auditd EXECVE in the standard schema carries no parent-process attribution to anchor on redis-server. Cross-checked against: • https://redis.io/blog/security-advisory-cve202623479-cve202625243-cve-2026-25588-cve202625589-cve-2026-23631/ • https://github.com/berabuddies/redis-poc • https://github.com/RedisBloom/RedisBloom/security/advisories/GHSA-7862-34pw-44wv
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Redis Sentinel notification-script / client-reconfig-script, which legitimately spawn /bin/sh on failover events
  • Container entrypoints where redis-server is PID1 and forks a healthcheck shell (redis-cli ping wrapped in sh)
  • Custom Redis modules (e.g. RedisGears) that legitimately shell out for their runtime
  • Ops backup/maintenance wrappers invoked under the redis service account
  • BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF forks (same-name child, excluded by the child list but visible to analysts triaging the process tree)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("notification-script","client-reconfig-script") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "sentinel")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the flagged redis-server PID — inspect the child command line for reverse-shell/download patterns (bash -i, /dev/tcp, curl|sh) and confirm the host runs an unpatched branch (6.2.22/7.4.9/8.6.4/8.8.0/8.8.1). Rule out Sentinel notification-script by checking redis.conf. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child, and immediately apply `ACL SETUSER default -restore` (or revoke RESTORE from all non-admin ACLs) and block untrusted network access to 6379/6380. 3) Hunt: pivot to any outbound connections and file writes (cron/authorized_keys) from that redis-server PID, and sweep the fleet for the same parent→shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "redis-server"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","ssh","scp","curl","wget","php")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "redis-server"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/python","/perl","/ruby","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/ssh","/scp","/curl","/wget","/php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Redis Server Spawning Shell or Interpreter (RESTORE RCE Payoff)

status: experimental

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="redis-server" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","ssh","scp","curl","wget","php")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unpatched Redis / RedisBloom exact-version exposure (no-CVE July 2026 RCE branches) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running the exact Redis branch versions the published PoCs target (6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, 8.8.0, 8.8.1). Because Redis assigned no new CVE for the July shared-NACK and TDigest bugs, vulnerability scanners keyed on CveId miss them — exact version-string matching is the only reliable exposure hunt, exactly as the article warns ('check the exact branch version'). Rationale: The article's core operational point is that 6.2.22 and 7.4.9 were the May 'fixed' destination but still lack the shared-NACK guard, and that no July CVE exists — so CVE-based scanning is blind and exact-version inventory matching is required. Versions taken directly from the article and confirmed in the berabuddies PoC repo title. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/berabuddies/redis-poc • https://github.com/redis/redis/releases/tag/8.6.5
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host mid-upgrade briefly reporting the old version in a cached inventory snapshot
  • RedisBloom bundled inside 8.8.x reported as a separate 'redis' software entry, double-counting a single host
  • Dev/test Redis instances that are intentionally pinned and network-isolated (still exposed if reachable)
  • Vendor-repackaged Redis (e.g. Bitnami/RHEL) whose version string appends a distro suffix and evades exact match — treat as a coverage gap, widen with `has` if needed
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, confirm the branch and whether the instance is network-reachable from untrusted segments and whether RESTORE is permitted for any non-admin ACL. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the fixed release for the branch (6.2.23/7.2.15/7.4.10/8.2.8/8.4.5/8.6.5/8.8.1); as an interim, `ACL SETUSER` to revoke RESTORE from accounts that don't need it and firewall 6379/6380. 3) Hunt: on any flagged host, retro-hunt redis-server child-shell spawns, cron/authorized_keys writes, and outbound public connections to check for prior exploitation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "redis"
| where SoftwareVersion in ("6.2.22","7.4.9","8.6.4","8.8.0","8.8.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "redis"
| where SoftwareVersion in ("6.2.22","7.4.9","8.6.4","8.8.0","8.8.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc
redis-server writing to cron or SSH authorized_keys (post-RCE persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the redis-server process writing into cron directories or an authorized_keys file — the canonical persistence step following a Redis RCE. Grounded in the article's 'built RCE exploit' outcome: once system() runs under the redis UID, attackers commonly drop a cron job or SSH key for durable access. Rationale: The redis-server binary has no legitimate reason to write cron files or authorized_keys; pairing the initiating process (redis-server) with these two persistence sinks yields a very-low-FP, high-severity follow-on to the article's RCE. Datadog empty: standard linux.auditd schema exposes no target-file-path field to key on. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/berabuddies/redis-poc • https://redis.io/blog/security-advisory-cve202623479-cve202625243-cve-2026-25588-cve202625589-cve-2026-23631/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured Redis writing its dump.rdb/appendonly file into an unusual directory (excluded here — not cron/ssh — but analysts may see adjacent noise)
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) running under the redis service account deploying an ops SSH key
  • Container image build steps that seed authorized_keys while redis is the entrypoint
  • Legacy cron-based Redis backup jobs installed under the redis UID
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in ("ansible","puppet","salt") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the written content — inspect the cron line or the injected SSH public key, and correlate its timestamp with any redis-server child-shell or unpatched-version finding on the host. 2) Contain: remove the cron entry / key, isolate the host, rotate the redis account, and revoke RESTORE via ACL. 3) Hunt: search other Redis hosts for identical cron commands or the same SSH public key, and check for successful SSH logons using that key across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "redis-server"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab")) or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "redis-server"
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab")) or (TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
