Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or SHA1 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e") or MD5 in~ ("c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c010f64080b0b0997b362a8e6b9c618e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash

msaRAT: MSI impersonating Windows update executed from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe executing an MSI dropped to C:\ProgramData whose name/property info impersonates a Windows update, matching Chaos ransomware's msaRAT delivery where a custom action loads the RAT DLL straight into memory. Article-specific: the installer masquerades as a Windows update and lives in ProgramData rather than a signed update path. Rationale: Uses the article's exact delivery: an MSI in ProgramData impersonating a Windows update executed by msiexec, with a memory-loading custom action. Cross-checked against Talos full report and The Hacker News which confirm the installer property info impersonates a Windows update. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software packaged as an MSI staged in ProgramData by a legitimate installer bootstrapper
  • Enterprise software distribution (SCCM/Intune) caching update MSIs under ProgramData vendor folders
  • Driver/firmware update utilities (Dell, Lenovo, HP) that stage MSIs named with 'Update' in ProgramData
  • Legitimate Windows optional-feature MSIs referenced with KB numbers in command line
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full msiexec command line and the MSI file hash; check the parent process and whether the MSI is signed and by whom (msaRAT installer is unsigned/impersonates Windows). Query DeviceImageLoadEvents for a DLL loaded by msiexec.exe from ProgramData at the same time. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the msiexec/child process tree, and block the MSI hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: Look on the same host for a preceding curl.exe download to ProgramData and subsequent headless chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging flags (msaRAT CDP C2).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT MSI Impersonating Windows Update from ProgramData

msaRAT: curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData AIDelivery High
Detects curl.exe (or wget) retrieving a .msi to C:\ProgramData, the exact ingress step Talos describes for Chaos ransomware's msaRAT before the fake Windows-update installer runs. Article-specific: correlates the curl download with the msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling infra. Rationale: Directly implements Talos's 'monitor for unusual curl commands downloading MSI files to ProgramData' guidance, anchored on the confirmed delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling domain. Corroborated by The Hacker News and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or DevOps scripts using curl to fetch MSI installers into a working directory under ProgramData
  • Software packaging/CI agents downloading MSI artifacts to a ProgramData staging cache
  • Admin manually fetching a vendor MSI with curl for testing
  • Chocolatey/winget-style tooling that shells out to curl for package retrieval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("choco.exe","winget.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "workers.dev" == false)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Extract the full download URL from the curl command line and check reputation of the host/IP; confirm the destination path in ProgramData and whether the resulting MSI was subsequently executed by msiexec. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, block the URL/IP (172.86.126.18) and workers.dev signaling domain at proxy/firewall, and quarantine the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: Search the host and org for the same URL/IP in DeviceNetworkEvents and for a following headless browser launch with --remote-debugging (msaRAT C2 stage).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wget.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\" or CommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT curl Download of MSI to ProgramData

msaRAT: Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe spawned with --remote-debugging-port/--remote-debugging-pipe (and typically --headless) by a non-interactive parent, the mechanism msaRAT uses to drive a browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol for covert C2. Article-specific: the RAT starts its own headless browser instance and controls it via CDP rather than touching the network directly. Rationale: Targets the CDP-driven headless browser msaRAT spawns for C2 (Talos: 'implement behavioral monitoring to catch Chrome DevTools Protocol abuse'). Confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News that the RAT starts Chrome/Edge in headless mode and drives it over CDP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Puppeteer, Playwright, Selenium headless) run by developers or CI runners
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services that drive headless Chromium
  • Lighthouse/synthetic-monitoring agents launching headless Edge/Chrome
  • Electron-based apps invoking a bundled Chromium with debugging pipe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","lighthouse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the parent process that launched the headless browser and its binary path/signature; a browser started by an unsigned/unknown parent (not a dev tool, IDE, or CI agent) is high-suspicion. Check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) debugging listener. 2) Contain: If the parent is untrusted, isolate the host and kill the browser + parent tree. 3) Hunt: Pivot from the host to DeviceNetworkEvents for browser egress to workers.dev / STUN (3478) / Twilio TURN, and back to any preceding msiexec-from-ProgramData execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Headless, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = CommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Headless, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Headless Browser Launched with Remote Debugging (msaRAT CDP C2)

msaRAT: Connection to Chaos delivery IP / workers.dev signaling relay AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the msaRAT delivery server 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP over port 443) or the Cloudflare workers.dev signaling relay is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev. Article-specific: these are the confirmed network IOCs for msaRAT's payload delivery and WebRTC signaling. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the confirmed msaRAT delivery server (172.86.126.18, plain HTTP over 443) and the workers.dev signaling relay, both published in the Talos report and echoed by Security Affairs/Help Net Security. High-fidelity, low-FP IOC alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign traffic to an unrelated tenant sharing the ols-img-12.workers.dev Cloudflare Worker subdomain (unlikely but possible if the subdomain is later repurposed)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the sample and generating IOC contact from a research host
  • Threat-intel enrichment or IOC-validation scanners in the environment reaching the IP
  • Stale IOC after infrastructure takedown produces sinkhole hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process — a browser (chrome/msedge) reaching workers.dev or any process reaching 172.86.126.18 on 443; confirm whether traffic to the IP is plain HTTP despite the 443 port (protocol mismatch is a strong indicator). 2) Contain: Block the IP and domain at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the process tree. 3) Hunt: On the host, look for the preceding curl→ProgramData MSI download, msiexec fake-update execution, and a headless browser launched with --remote-debugging; sweep the org for any other host that contacted either IOC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "172.86.126.18" or DstHostname =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or Url has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT: Headless browser initiating WebRTC STUN/TURN egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe making STUN/TURN connections (ports 3478/5349) when the browser was launched non-interactively with debugging/headless flags — the WebRTC data-channel egress msaRAT relays through Twilio TURN for C2. Article-specific: msaRAT sends a STUN request then tunnels C2 over WebRTC from its own headless browser, not user-driven WebRTC. Rationale: Targets msaRAT's WebRTC egress (STUN request + Twilio TURN relay) constrained to a headless/CDP-driven browser so it isn't just generic WebRTC noise. Talos, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News confirm the STUN-then-WebRTC-via-Twilio C2 path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate video conferencing / VoIP in-browser (Google Meet, Teams web, Discord web) using WebRTC STUN/TURN
  • Browser-based screen-sharing or WebRTC test pages initiated by a user
  • Puppeteer/Playwright automation that legitimately exercises WebRTC
  • Corporate SBC/collaboration platforms relaying media over 3478/5349
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the browser was launched non-interactively (parent is not explorer.exe and command line carries --headless/--remote-debugging); user-driven Meet/Teams WebRTC will have an interactive parent and no debugging flags. 2) Contain: If non-interactive, isolate the host, kill the browser + parent, and block the TURN destination and the workers.dev signaling domain. 3) Hunt: Correlate on the host with the CDP browser-launch detection, contact to 172.86.126.18 / workers.dev, and the fake-update MSI chain; check for Chaos ransomware staging (shadow-copy deletion, RMM tools).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where RemotePort in (3478, 5349)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3478, 5349)
| where NetworkProtocol has_any ("UDP","TCP")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) · [LLM] Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hidden PowerShell pulls installer.exe from pixeldrain.com to %Temp% (self-deleting dropper) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS contact to Q2 2026 campaign infrastructure (pixeldrain payload + ClickUp dropper hosts) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email from the DKIM-signed operator domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (sender Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) used in Microsoft's Q2 2026 multi-stage campaign that lured users with a fake 'Internal Affairs – Financials & Staff Updates' message. This is the delivery anchor of the chain that ends in silent malware execution via ClickUp and pixeldrain. Rationale: Anchors on the exact sender domain (9i6pokerdepot.com) and full address (Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) from the article's IOC table; a niche gambling-themed domain sending to enterprise mailboxes is effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team deliberately replays the IOC domain in a phishing-simulation/purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel or sandbox tooling that re-sends captured campaign samples into a test mailbox
  • A researcher forwarding the original email internally for analysis (appears as intra-org, not inbound)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all recipients of the message via NetworkMessageId; check DeliveryLocation (Inbox vs Quarantine) and whether any user opened it. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide with an EmailPostDelivery/ZAP action and block 9i6pokerdepot.com at the mail gateway and Safe Links. 3) Hunt: for every recipient, pivot to UC2/UC3 — look for Financial_report.bat writes and PowerShell contacting pixeldrain.com on their devices in the following 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host AIDelivery High
Detects the stage-2 batch dropper (Financial_report.bat) written to disk with a download origin of clickup-attachments.com — the trusted-service hop the Q2 2026 campaign used after a login.microsoftonline.com redirect. ClickUp's public attachment host serving a .bat file is the article-specific tell. Rationale: Uses the exact dropper filename (Financial_report.bat) and the trusted-service host (clickup-attachments.com, subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com) from the article and corroborating write-up; a .bat sourced from ClickUp is not a legitimate business pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/

1) Triage: on the flagged host, capture the SHA256 of Financial_report.bat and the InitiatingProcess (browser/Outlook) that wrote it; confirm the FileOriginUrl subdomain. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the .bat already executed (check for cmd.exe→powershell.exe children); block clickup-attachments.com download paths at proxy and delete the file. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host/user for PowerShell referencing pixeldrain.com and installer.exe in %Temp%.

Hidden PowerShell pulls installer.exe from pixeldrain.com to %Temp% (self-deleting dropper) AIInstallation High
Detects the final-stage behaviour of the Q2 2026 chain: Financial_report.bat spawning a hidden PowerShell that downloads installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into the user's Temp directory, runs it with a silent flag, then deletes the dropper. Anchored on the pixeldrain download string in a hidden-window PowerShell command line. Rationale: Combines the concrete C2/payload host (pixeldrain.com, file id 3v92oJiL) and behaviour (hidden PowerShell fetching installer.exe into %Temp%) from the article plus the corroborating write-up; pixeldrain in a PowerShell download command line is a high-fidelity, near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scripting a download of a shared file from pixeldrain.com via PowerShell
  • Red-team/atomic-test emulation of T1105 ingress transfer using pixeldrain as the staging host
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a monitored VM (expected in a sandbox segment)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe","outlook.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hidden","installer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is cmd.exe running Financial_report.bat and inspect the full command line for the pixeldrain URL and the %Temp% output path/installer.exe name. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the PowerShell and installer.exe process tree, block pixeldrain.com egress, and preserve %Temp% for the dropped/deleted installer. 3) Hunt: sweep for installer.exe executed from %Temp% with a silent flag across the fleet and check DeviceNetworkEvents for other hosts contacting pixeldrain.com or the ClickUp subdomain (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pixeldrain.com" or ProcessCommandLine has "3v92oJiL"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("installer.exe","\\Temp\\","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-nop","downloadfile","invoke-webrequest","iwr","curl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "pixeldrain.com" or CommandLine has "3v92oJiL"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network/DNS contact to Q2 2026 campaign infrastructure (pixeldrain payload + ClickUp dropper hosts) AICommand & Control High
Endpoint-agnostic sweep for any host resolving or connecting to the specific campaign hosts — pixeldrain.com/api/file/3v92oJiL (final payload) and t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com (BAT dropper). Catches the chain even where PowerShell/script-block logging is disabled, using DNS and network egress telemetry. Rationale: Uses the exact payload URL (pixeldrain.com/api/file/3v92oJiL) and dropper subdomain (t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com) from the article's IOC table; direct-to-IOC network/DNS contact is a resilient, near-zero-FP confirmation that survives host log gaps. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Auth.js server-configuration error reaching production (fail-open precondition) AIExploitation High
Hunts application/stdout logs for the specific Auth.js v5 configuration-error strings that flip the `auth()` object from null to a truthy error object, causing `!!auth` checks to fail open for every request. The article itself recommends treating any `[auth][error]` line as a failed health check, so this is the root-cause detection. Rationale: Uses the exact Auth.js error identifiers named in the advisory (`[auth][error]`, `InvalidEndpoints`, `MissingSecret`) plus the user-facing server-config error string; all four confirmed as real Auth.js error classes via authjs.dev/reference/core/errors and upstream issue #11934. These strings only emit when the config is broken, i.e. exactly when the fail-open condition is active. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934 • https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-8FPG-XM3F-6CX3
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/staging/preview deployments intentionally running with incomplete provider config emit [auth][error] routinely
  • CI builds surfacing MissingSecret during Next.js build since 5.0.0-beta.16 (upstream issue #10538)
  • A newly added OAuth provider misconfigured on a non-production branch preview
  • Log aggregation of test/debug output that quotes the error string verbatim
  • Deliberate DR/chaos testing of auth failure modes
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "preview" and Computer !has "-ci"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the emitting host is production (not dev/preview). If prod, the app is currently fail-open — every visitor is treated as authenticated. Check the timestamp: has this host served traffic since the first error line? 2) CONTAIN: Roll back the offending deploy or restore the missing env var (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer). If rollback is slow, take the affected instance out of the load balancer. 3) HUNT: Pull all successful requests to protected routes on that host since FirstSeen (see the fail-open exploitation UC) to scope who accessed what while auth was broken; review for sensitive-data or privileged-action access.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    or SyslogMessage has "InvalidEndpoints"
    or SyslogMessage has "MissingSecret"
    or SyslogMessage has "There was a problem with the server configuration"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), SampleMessage=any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Auth.js Server-Configuration Error Reaching Production (Fail-Open Precondition)
id: b3f1c2a4-7d9e-4a1b-8c2d-1f4e6a9b0c31
description: Detects Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-configuration error strings in application logs. These errors populate the auth() object with a truthy error, causing existence-based auth checks (!!auth) to fail open (GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3
  - https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: application
  product: nodejs
detection:
  selection:
    message|contains:
      - '[auth][error]'
      - 'InvalidEndpoints'
      - 'MissingSecret'
      - 'There was a problem with the server configuration'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:nodejs ("[auth][error]" OR InvalidEndpoints OR MissingSecret OR "There was a problem with the server configuration")
# log group: /aws/lambda/*  (Next.js SSR / API-route function stdout)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/ or @message like /InvalidEndpoints/ or @message like /MissingSecret/ or @message like /There was a problem with the server configuration/
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
index=* ("[auth][error]" OR "InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "There was a problem with the server configuration")
| stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen count values(source) as sources by host
| convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)
| sort - lastSeen
Auth.js fail-open exploited: protected routes served 200/302 during an active auth-error window AIExploitation Medium
Correlates Auth.js `[auth][error]` log lines with successful (200/302) HTTP responses on the same host inside a short window — the observable signature of the app granting access while the auth layer is broken. This catches the vulnerability being exploited (unauthenticated visitors served protected content), not just the misconfiguration. Rationale: Ties the article's exact fail-open string (`[auth][error]`) to served-content status codes (200/302) on the same host within 10 minutes — the mechanism the advisory describes (`!!auth` true for every request while broken). Correlation on host + time isolates the exploitation from the mere presence of the error. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934 • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-8FPG-XM3F-6CX3
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately authenticated users receiving 200/302 during the same window as a transient auth error
  • Uptime/health-check probes hitting genuinely public routes returning 200
  • Static asset requests (js/css/img) returning 200 unrelated to auth-gated routes
  • A single transient OAuth provider timeout logged as [auth][error] while auth otherwise functions normally
Suppression filter
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".ico" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".svg" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the 200/302 responses are to auth-protected routes (not public pages or static assets). Correlate cIP against known-authenticated sessions — unrecognised IPs receiving protected content during the error window are the strongest signal. 2) CONTAIN: If protected content was served to unauthenticated callers, roll back/fix the config (restore AUTH_SECRET or provider issuer) and pull the host from rotation; invalidate any sessions issued during the window. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every distinct src IP served 200 during all error windows on this host; check downstream logs for data export, privileged mutations, or account-takeover actions performed under the fail-open.
let ErrWindow = 10m;
let AuthErrors = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | project ErrTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AuthError = SyslogMessage;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where scStatus in (200, 302)
| where csMethod in ("GET","POST")
| join kind=inner AuthErrors on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (ErrTime .. ErrTime + ErrWindow)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, ErrTime, AuthError
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
`summariesonly`
| tstats count, values(Web.uri_path) as uri_paths, values(Web.src) as src_ips from datamodel=Web where (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=302) by Web.dest, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner dest [ search index=* ("[auth][error]" OR "MissingSecret" OR "InvalidEndpoints") | stats count by host | rename host as dest | fields dest ]
| sort - _time
summariesonly=false
| tstats count, values(Web.uri_path) as uri_paths, values(Web.src) as src_ips from datamodel=Web where (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=302) by Web.dest, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner dest [ search index=* ("[auth][error]" OR "MissingSecret" OR "InvalidEndpoints") | stats count by host | rename host as dest | fields dest ]
| sort - _time
Auth.js config break on deploy: first-ever [auth][error] on a previously-healthy host AIExploitation High
Baseline anti-join that surfaces the exact moment a previously-working deployment becomes misconfigured — the article's named trigger ('an environment variable is changed or removed during a deploy'). Flags hosts emitting `[auth][error]` for the first time versus a 14-day baseline, catching the silent transition from fail-closed to fail-open. Rationale: Directly targets the advisory's stated risk narrative — a deploy removing/altering an env var flips a healthy app to fail-open. The 14-day baseline anti-join on `[auth][error]` isolates the first-time-broken transition, which is far higher-fidelity for prod than any-occurrence matching (dev noise typically pre-exists in the baseline). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • First deployment of a brand-new app/host with no prior baseline (expected initial errors)
  • Host re-imaged or renamed so it appears 'new' though auth was already broken
  • Blue/green or autoscale instance coming online mid-rollout with a transient config gap
  • Baseline window shorter than an intermittent provider's error cadence, so a rare blip reads as first-seen
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "preview" and Computer !has "-ci"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm this host had a healthy 14-day baseline and just started erroring — check whether a deploy/config change landed immediately before FirstSeen (CI/CD timeline, env-var change history). 2) CONTAIN: Treat as an active fail-open on a production host: roll back the deploy or restore the missing config value, and remove the instance from the load balancer until auth() returns null-on-failure again. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the fail-open exploitation UC for this host/window to enumerate what was accessed unauthenticated between FirstSeen and remediation; verify no privileged actions or data reads occurred.
let Baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | summarize by Computer;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Computer
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), SampleMessage=any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
APPLICATION
index=* "[auth][error]" earliest=-1d
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen count values(source) as sources by host
| where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(), "-1d")
| join type=leftanti host [ search index=* "[auth][error]" earliest=-14d latest=-1d | stats count by host | fields host ]
| convert ctime(firstSeen)
| sort - firstSeen

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound HTML-attachment lure exploiting Zimbra XSS (CVE-2025-66376) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration exposed to CVE-2025-66376 (Void Blizzard target) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CL-STA-1114 (Void Blizzard) Zimbra espionage C2/exfil infrastructure contact · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser-initiated webmail data exfiltration to CL-STA-1114 C2 · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
CL-STA-1114 (Void Blizzard) Zimbra espionage C2/exfil infrastructure contact AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the nine hard-coded C2 domains or nine C2 IPs used by CL-STA-1114 / Void Blizzard to receive stolen Zimbra webmail data (credentials, 2FA scratch codes, CSRF tokens, 90-day mail archive). Article-specific because it matches the exact IOC set Unit 42 attributes to this campaign, not a generic beacon shape. Rationale: Uses the exact nine C2 domains and nine C2 IPs Unit 42 attributes to CL-STA-1114; cross-checked against CISA AA26-204A and The Hacker News which independently confirm the Void Blizzard/LAUNDRY BEAR Zimbra campaign, so the IOCs meet the two-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html • https://cyberscoop.com/russian-laundry-bear-zimbra-exploit/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating the same IOCs from a research host
  • Security scanner / EDR retro-hunt actively probing the IOC list
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS appliance logging the resolution before blocking
  • A legitimately-registered look-alike domain reclaimed post-takedown resolving to benign parking infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs. service); confirm the user has an active Zimbra webmail session and whether the org runs unpatched ZCS (<10.0.18 / <10.1.13). 2) Contain: block all nine domains/IPs at proxy+DNS, isolate the host, and force-reset the affected user's Zimbra password and 2FA scratch codes (the payload steals both). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/device for the last 90 days of mailbox access, search all endpoints for any of the nine IOCs, and review Zimbra logs for the CSS @import XSS mail that triggered it.
